title: Jonah sulks (Jonah 4)
hookLine: angry at God's mercy, Jonah mourns a shady plant; God asks: shouldn't I pity Nineveh?
carry: mercy is wider than you like

lines: IT SHOULD END AT CHAPTER THREE.
cards: If the book of Jonah were a movie, it would end after chapter three. The city repents, God relents, roll credits. But there's a fourth chapter, and it opens with the prophet furious.
In the King James Bible: "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry." He's just watched a whole city turn at five words, and he's livid. Then he finally tells God why he ran.
Not fear of the storm, or of the Assyrians. Something much more uncomfortable. He was afraid God would be kind.

teach.b: His complaint sounds almost like a hymn: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness." Those words echo God's own self-description to Moses on the mountain in Exodus.
Jonah knows the creed by heart. He just hates that it applies to Nineveh.

teach.h: DOEST THOU WELL TO BE ANGRY?
teach.b: So he asks to die, and God answers with a short, gentle question: "Doest thou well to be angry?" Jonah doesn't reply. He walks out east of the city, builds a little shelter, and sits to see what will become of it.
Then the comic part. God makes a leafy plant grow up overnight to shade his head. The King James calls it a gourd; nobody is quite sure what plant the Hebrew means.

teach.h: GLAD OF A GOURD, THEN A WORM.
teach.b: And Jonah "was exceeding glad of the gourd." The one time the book calls him glad, it's over shade.
Next morning God sends a worm, the plant withers, the sun beats down, a hot east wind blows, and Jonah wants to die again, this time over a plant.
God makes his point: you pitied a plant you didn't plant or grow, which came up in a night and died in a night.
Should I not pity Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?

teach.h: THE BOOK ENDS ON A QUESTION.
teach.b: The book ends there, on a question.
We never hear Jonah's answer; some readers hear that silence as an invitation. And the last words in English are much cattle. God's mercy, in this book, reaches even the cows.

how: Some Christians read Jonah 4 alongside Jesus's parable of the prodigal son, where the older brother also resents a welcome; sermons pair them to ask how people respond to mercy shown to others.

games.q: you're Jonah. your enemies were spared, your shade plant just died, and God asks: is it right for you to be angry? what does the book say you answer?
o: yes, I'm right to be angry.
games.why: the book ends on God's question about Nineveh and much cattle. Jonah's answer is left blank, and some readers hear it as theirs to give.

practice: Think of a time someone got off easy and it bothered you, a coworker who wasn't fired, a sibling forgiven too fast, and let the irritation come up without judging it; Jonah felt it too.
Then hear God's question, as gently as the story asks it: is it right for you to be angry? If you pray, bring it to God honestly, as Jonah did; if not, notice where it lives in your body.

wordCard.voice: Jonah sulks. Angry that God spared his enemies, glad of a shady plant, and left facing a question the book never lets him answer.

orig.note: Hebrew: gracious. the first word of God's description in Jonah's complaint, the creed he knew by heart, and resented.
